n: Elihu’s third speech is short. He addresses whether righteousness gets Job anything from God.
Elihu asks whether Job really thinks it’s right to say his own righteousness outweighs God’s.

f.w: My righteousness is more than God's
f.g: Or “I am in the right before God” — Elihu presses Job’s words to an extreme.

n: He quotes Job as asking, “What good does it do me not to sin?”
Elihu promises to answer both Job and his friends.

f.g: Possibly the three friends, or anyone who shares Job’s view.

n: Look up at the sky and the clouds, so much higher than you — God is far higher still.
If you sin, how does that hurt God? Even many sins don’t harm him.
If you are righteous, what do you give him? What does he gain from you? God is not dependent on us.
Your sin or goodness mainly affects other people like you. Our choices deeply touch those around us.

f.w: thy righteousness may profit the son of man

n: People cry out under oppression and plead for help against the powerful.
But no one asks, “Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night?” They cry for relief but don’t seek God himself.
It is God who teaches us more than animals and makes us wiser than birds.

f.w: wiser than the fowls of heaven

n: They cry out but get no answer because of their pride.
God does not listen to empty cries, and the Almighty ignores them.
Even when Job says he can’t see God, his case is before him — so Job should wait for him.
Elihu suggests that because God has not yet punished in anger, Job thinks God doesn’t notice wrongdoing.

f.w: he knoweth it not in great extremity
f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; possibly “he takes little notice of folly.”

n: So Elihu concludes Job is opening his mouth in empty talk and piling up words without knowledge.
